title_en: Xie Yeyang v. Shanghai Zoo — dispute over injury caused by a domestic animal
ruling_gist_en: Article 81 of the Tort Liability Law clearly stipulates no-fault liability for zoos, while also providing that if the victim or guardian is indeed at fault, the zoo may be relieved of liability, either in part or in full. As a professional institution that raises and manages animals, the zoo has a duty of care and management according to law, and its safety facilities should fully take into account the special safety needs of minors to eliminate harmful consequences to the greatest extent. Visitors should also behave civilly in the park, and guardians must fulfill their guardianship duties; otherwise, they shall bear corresponding liability according to law.

full_text_en:
Xie Yeyang v. Shanghai Zoo
— Dispute over Injury Caused by Domesticated Animal

[Ruling Summary]

Article 81 of the Tort Liability Law clearly stipulates the no-fault liability of zoos. At the same time, it provides that if the victim or the guardian is actually at fault, the zoo may be relieved of liability or its liability may be reduced. As a professional institution that keeps and manages animals, a zoo has a duty of care and management in accordance with the law. Its safety facilities should fully take into account the special safety needs of minors, so as to minimize the occurrence of harmful consequences. Visitors shall also visit the zoo in a civilized manner, and guardians shall fulfill their guardianship duties; otherwise, they shall also bear corresponding responsibility according to law.

Plaintiff: Xie Yeyang, male, 5 years old, Han ethnicity, registered domicile: Xingfuzhou Administrative Village, Nicha Town, Wuwei County, Anhui Province, current residence: Minzhu Village, Xujing Town, Qingpu District, Shanghai.

Legal Representative: Xie Yuping, father of the plaintiff Xie Yeyang, male, 37 years old, Han ethnicity, address same as above.

Legal Representative: Xu Shimei, mother of the plaintiff Xie Yeyang, female, 37 years old, Han ethnicity, address same as above.

Defendant: Shanghai Zoo, domicile: Hongqiao Road, Changning District, Shanghai.

Legal Representative: Zhang Feng, Director of the Zoo.

The plaintiff, Xie Yeyang, filed a lawsuit with the Changning District People's Court of Shanghai against the defendant, Shanghai Zoo, regarding a dispute over injury caused by a domesticated animal.

The plaintiff, Xie Yeyang, and his legal representatives, Xie Yuping and Xu Shimei, alleged: At about 3:00 p.m. on April 10, 2011, the plaintiff and his parents were visiting the defendant Shanghai Zoo. When they arrived at the monkey exhibition area, while the plaintiff was feeding food to the monkeys, the middle finger of his right hand was bitten by a monkey. Neither before nor during the incident did any staff member of the defendant appear. Afterwards, the plaintiff and his parents reported the incident to the police on their own and took the plaintiff to Shanghai Children's Hospital for medical treatment. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant had failed to fulfill its duty of patrol, its management skills were unqualified, and the protective facilities were defective, allowing the plaintiff to crawl in at will. Therefore, the defendant was at fault. The plaintiff requested the defendant to compensate: medical expenses of RMB (hereinafter) 4,058.09, transportation expenses of RMB 408, hospitalization food subsidy of RMB 160, moral damages of RMB 40,000, and attorney's fees of RMB 8,000. During the litigation, the plaintiff amended the claims: medical expenses of RMB 4,058.09, transportation expenses of RMB 408, hospitalization food subsidy of RMB 160, disability compensation of RMB 63,676, nursing expenses of RMB 6,600, nutrition expenses of RMB 1,500, prosthetic costs of RMB 2,300, remaining prosthetic costs before age 18 of RMB 13,800, prosthetic costs for 20 years after age 18 of RMB 11,500, prosthetic maintenance costs of RMB 3,910, judicial appraisal fees of RMB 1,930, attorney's fees of RMB 8,000, and moral damages of RMB 50,000.

The defendant Shanghai Zoo argued: It had no objection to the time and place of the plaintiff Xie Yeyang's injury. However, it contended that: First, the defendant had fulfilled its duty of safety to a reasonable extent and had established comprehensive safety rules for visitors. 1. Protective measures were adequate. The biting monkey was confined in a metal mesh cage, which provided the first layer of protection; outside the cage, there was a metal railing about 1.20 meters high with an isolation area of 1.50 meters (the distance from the cage to the railing), which served as a second layer of protection, preventing visitors from getting close to the animals, and also as a warning that visitors should not approach the cage. 2. The defendant had fulfilled its warning and notification obligation. At the zoo entrance, the defendant posted notices requiring parents to supervise their children, prohibiting teasing, feeding animals, climbing over railings, etc., with illustrated safety warning signs. 3. The defendant's staff had fulfilled their patrol duties. On the day of the incident, staff were on duty and patrolling the zoo normally. Although no staff member was at the location of the plaintiff's injury at the time, the injury occurred in an instant, and the zoo area is large; it is impossible for the defendant's staff to be present to prevent incidents at all times. The prevention of such dangers mainly relies on visitors' civilized conduct, supplemented by mobile duty personnel and written notices to discourage uncivilized behavior. Requiring the defendant to have fixed supervisory posts at every scenic spot around the clock would exceed the reasonable safety limit. 4. Regarding the gaps in the protective railing. The protective railing itself serves as a warning and deterrent, not as an obstacle for children to crawl through. The defendant had installed a dense metal mesh cage, which children cannot penetrate, thus providing safety protection. Second, the cause of the plaintiff's injury was the plaintiff's failure to comply with the zoo rules and the failure of the plaintiff's legal representatives to fulfill their supervisory duties. Therefore, the plaintiff and his legal representatives should bear full responsibility. The direct cause of the injury was the plaintiff feeding the monkey in the cage with his hand; the indirect cause was the failure of the plaintiff's legal representatives to fulfill their guardianship duties, allowing the plaintiff to go through the protective railing. The plaintiff's legal representatives failed to provide safety education to the plaintiff in advance and failed to stop the plaintiff's behavior in time. The plaintiff's legal representatives were seriously negligent. In light of the above, the defendant disagreed with compensating the plaintiff for the relevant losses.

The Changning District People's Court of Shanghai found at first instance:

On the morning of April 10, 2011, the plaintiff Xie Yeyang and his parents visited the defendant Shanghai Zoo. At about 3:00 p.m. that day, when the plaintiff and his family arrived at the primate exhibition area, the plaintiff passed through the protective railing set up outside the cage and, while feeding food to the monkeys, the middle finger of his right hand was bitten by a monkey. At the time of the incident, no staff member of Shanghai Zoo was present. After the plaintiff's father complained to the relevant department of the zoo, due to the urgency of the situation, he took the plaintiff to Shanghai Children's Hospital for medical treatment on his own and reported the matter to the police. The plaintiff was hospitalized on the same day and was discharged on April 13, 2011. After discharge, the plaintiff received follow-up treatment at the Qibao Community Health Service Center, Minhang District, Shanghai, near his home. The plaintiff incurred medical expenses of RMB 4,058.09 (including hospitalization meal costs of RMB 32.50). On December 13, 2011, the plaintiff had a prosthetic fitted for his right middle finger at Shanghai Kesheng Prosthetics Co., Ltd., costing RMB 2,300. After an expert consultation by Shanghai Kesheng Prosthetics Co., Ltd., it was confirmed that the plaintiff needed to replace the prosthetic every two years until the age of 18, and every four years after reaching adulthood, with annual maintenance costs amounting to 5% of the total prosthetic cost. The recommended compensation period for the prosthetic was from the date of first fitting until 20 years after the plaintiff's adulthood.

Upon the application of the plaintiff Xie Yeyang, the court commissioned the Forensic Appraisal Center of the Institute of Forensic Science to conduct an appraisal of the plaintiff's injuries. The appraisal conclusion was: The plaintiff's right hand injury caused by the incident resulted in sequelae equivalent to a Grade 10 disability under road traffic accident standards. The nursing period for this injury was 60 days, and the nutrition period was 30 days.

During the trial, the court inspected the incident cage: The cage was made of iron mesh. At a distance of 2 meters from the cage, there were illustrated warning signs reading "Do Not Climb Over Railing," "Do Not Knock," "Do Not Tease," etc. A metal protective railing 1.12 meters high was built 1.50 meters away from the cage, with gaps of about 15 centimeters between the railings. On-site tests showed that the plaintiff Xie Yeyang and children under 10 years old (those who are thinner and smaller) could crawl through the gaps in the railing.

The above facts were confirmed by evidence including medical records, transportation expense receipts, household registration information, the Shanghai Public Security Bureau's case acceptance receipt, the expert opinion letter, the court's investigation record of Shanghai Kesheng Prosthetics Co., Ltd. on January 5, 2012, and the statements of the legal representatives of the plaintiff Xie Yeyang and the defendant Shanghai Zoo, and have been verified through court examination.

The issues in dispute at first instance were: First, whether the defendant Shanghai Zoo had fulfilled its management duties to be exempted from liability. Second, whether the plaintiff Xie Yeyang and his legal representatives were negligent, and whether the defendant's liability could be reduced. Third, the determination of the apportionment of liability.

The Changning District People's Court of Shanghai held at first instance:

I. Whether the defendant Shanghai Zoo had fulfilled its management duties to be exempted from liability. The defendant's management duties should be determined based on the specific type and nature of the animals. Moreover, given the unique social function of a zoo, it should not merely bear the duty of care of a prudent manager but should bear a higher duty of care consistent with its professional management of animals. This can be considered from the following aspects:
1. Whether it fulfilled its obligation to inform and warn. The defendant posted the "Shanghai Park Visiting Rules" at the zoo entrance and hung illustrated warning signs such as "Do Not Climb Over Railing," "Do Not Knock," and "Do Not Tease" at the primate house and other places. The plaintiff Xie Yeyang claimed that these warning signs were not present at the time of the incident and were poorly positioned, but the plaintiff provided no contrary evidence to support this claim; the court did not accept it. Moreover, as visitors approach the animals from a distance, the signs hung at a height of 2 meters are suitable for visitors to observe clearly from a distance, and the defendant had provided illustrated warnings easily recognizable by children; thus, it had fulfilled its obligation to inform.
2. Whether the management staff had a patrol system and had fulfilled their duty to dissuade visitors from climbing over or going through the railings to approach the animals. The duty rosters and feeder duty rosters provided by the defendant all showed that on the day of the incident, the defendant's employees were on duty and patrolling normally. The duty of care for a zoo should be determined based on the standard of a prudent and careful animal keeper under specific circumstances; it cannot be required to fulfill all duties of care. The plaintiff's injury occurred in an instant; it clearly cannot be demanded that the defendant's employees be present at the time. Therefore, the court found that the defendant had fulfilled its duty in terms of patrolling.
3. Whether there were safety issues with the facilities and equipment at the primate house. For a zoo, it is necessary to install special preventive equipment to isolate visitors from animals, preventing animals from harming others due to visitor provocation. The zoo should fulfill its necessary protective obligations to prevent pedestrians from accidentally entering the animal's reach and causing harm to others. The defendant had installed a mesh iron cage for the primates and added an external protective railing with a safe distance of 1.50 meters, which indeed provided some protection. However, the gaps of about 15 centimeters between the metal railings could only prevent adults from crawling through, not young children. The plaintiff went through the protective railing and fed the monkey with his hand, resulting in an injury to his right middle finger. A zoo is a public place open to the public, receiving thousands of preschool children every year. Based on its professional competence, it should have foreseen the possibility of such danger and failed to take necessary remedial measures. The zoo was at fault and had not fulfilled its management duties.

II. Whether the plaintiff Xie Yeyang and his legal representatives were negligent, and whether the defendant Shanghai Zoo's liability could be reduced. The direct cause of the plaintiff's injury was his violation of Article 23 of the "Shanghai Park Management Regulations": "Visitors shall visit parks in a civilized manner, protect park greenery, preserve park facilities, maintain park order, and comply with visiting rules..." and the "Shanghai Park Visiting Rules": "Do not tease... various animals..." and other relevant provisions. The plaintiff went through the protective railing without authorization and fed the monkey, resulting in injury; thus, the plaintiff was at fault. At the time of the incident, the plaintiff was only 4 years old, and his fault should be borne by his guardian. According to Article 18 of the "General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China," guardians shall fulfill their guardianship duties and protect the personal, property, and other lawful rights and interests of their wards. One of the guardian's duties is to protect the ward's person from harm. If, under the guardian's supervision, the ward, who has no capacity for civil conduct, suffers injury by his own actions or by the actions of others, it means the guardian has failed to fulfill their guardianship duties. In this case, the plaintiff was only 4 years old at the time of the incident, had no capacity for civil conduct, and lacked the cognitive ability and capacity to handle special situations regarding the danger of feeding monkeys. While it was not improper for the plaintiff's legal representatives to take him to the zoo, given the defendant's written warnings and notifications, the plaintiff's legal representatives nevertheless relaxed their duty to warn the plaintiff of dangers and to supervise him, leading to the plaintiff going through the protective railing and suffering injury. Therefore, the plaintiff's legal representatives were negligent in supervision, and the defendant's civil liability should be reduced.

III. The determination of the apportionment of liability. The plaintiff Xie Yeyang's legal representatives failed to properly supervise the plaintiff, who had no capacity for civil conduct, resulting in the plaintiff going through the protective railing without authorization and feeding the monkey. This was the proximate cause and primary cause of the plaintiff's injury, and they shall bear primary liability, i.e., 60% of the total compensation determined in this case. The defendant Shanghai Zoo's protective railing had safety defects that did not effectively prevent the plaintiff from going through, and it shall bear secondary liability, i.e., 40% of the total compensation determined in this case.

IV. Determination of the scope and amount of compensation. The compensation amount in this case should be reasonably determined based on the plaintiff Xie Yeyang's claims and laws and regulations.

1. Regarding medical expenses of RMB 4,058.09, both parties had no objection, and the court confirmed it. Based on the liability determination in this case, the court confirmed that the defendant Shanghai Zoo should bear RMB 1,623.24 of the plaintiff Xie Yeyang's medical expenses.

2. Transportation expenses of RMB 408. Transportation expenses are the actual expenses incurred by the plaintiff Xie Yeyang and his necessary accompanying personnel for seeking medical treatment or being transferred to another hospital. Based on the transportation expense receipts provided by the plaintiff, the time and place of medical treatment, the court discretionarily determined the amount to be RMB 380. Based on the liability determination in this case, the court discretionarily determined that the defendant Shanghai Zoo should bear RMB 152 of the plaintiff's transportation expenses.

3. Hospitalization food subsidy of RMB 160. The plaintiff Xie Yeyang's hospitalization food subsidy should be calculated at RMB 20 per day. The plaintiff was hospitalized for 3 days, and RMB 32.50 already included in the medical expenses should be deducted. Based on the liability determination in this case, the court confirmed that the defendant Shanghai Zoo should bear RMB 11 of the plaintiff's hospitalization food subsidy.

4. Regarding disability compensation of RMB 63,676, both parties had no objection. Based on the liability determination in this case, the court confirmed that the defendant Shanghai Zoo should bear RMB 25,470.40 of the plaintiff Xie Yeyang's disability compensation.

5. Nursing expenses of RMB 6,600. The evidence provided by the plaintiff Xie Yeyang regarding his father's loss of income due to nursing was insufficient and inconsistent with his statements in court. However, the plaintiff's nursing loss objectively existed as confirmed by judicial appraisal. The nursing standard could be referenced to the average monthly nursing standard in Shanghai, discretionarily determined to be RMB 2,000. Based on the liability determination in this case, the court discretionarily determined that the defendant Shanghai Zoo should bear RMB 1,600 of the plaintiff's nursing expenses.

6. Nutrition expenses of RMB 1,500. The court held that, considering the current living standard in Shanghai, the plaintiff Xie Yeyang's injury, and his age, the appropriate daily nutrition expense was RMB 40. Based on the liability determination in this case, the court discretionarily determined that the defendant Shanghai Zoo should bear RMB 480 of the plaintiff's nutrition expenses.

7. Prosthetic costs incurred on December 13, 2011, of RMB 2,300, remaining prosthetic costs before age 18 of RMB 13,800, prosthetic costs for 20 years after age 18 of RMB 11,500, and prosthetic maintenance costs of RMB 3,910. Although the plaintiff Xie Yeyang's prosthetic was cosmetic, considering that the injury to his right middle finger affected his ability to write and grasp objects, the prosthetic did serve a supplementary function for the plaintiff's right hand, helped meet his basic living needs, and appropriately alleviated his psychological pressure. Therefore, the court confirmed the prosthetic cost incurred on December 13, 2011. Based on the degree of fault of the defendant Shanghai Zoo, the court confirmed that the defendant should bear RMB 920. As for the remaining prosthetic costs claimed by the plaintiff, since they have not yet occurred, the time span for future occurrences is long, and the price range for prosthetic costs may change, for better protection of the plaintiff's lawful rights and interests, these costs may be claimed separately after actual occurrence.

8. Attorney's fees of RMB 8,000. The court held that this loss was actually incurred by the plaintiff Xie Yeyang for litigation and should be included in the compensation scope of this case. Based on the current attorney fee standards in Shanghai and the subject matter of this litigation, the attorney's fee could be discretionarily determined to be RMB 5,000. Based on the liability determination in this case, the court discretionarily determined that the defendant Shanghai Zoo should bear RMB 2,000 of the plaintiff's attorney's fees.

9. Moral damages of RMB 50,000. The court held that the plaintiff Xie Yeyang's injury indeed caused him significant mental and physical pain, resulting in a disability to the middle finger of his right hand with serious consequences, and moral damages should be awarded. Based on the liability determination in this case, the court discretionarily determined that the defendant Shanghai Zoo should pay the plaintiff moral damages of RMB 2,000.

10. Judicial appraisal fees of RMB 1,930. Based on the liability determination in this case, the defendant Shanghai Zoo should bear RMB 772 of the plaintiff Xie Yeyang's appraisal fees.

Accordingly, pursuant to Article 81, Article 26, Article 16, and Article 22 of the Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 18 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, the court rendered the following judgment on January 30, 2012:

1. The defendant Shanghai Zoo shall, within ten days after this judgment takes effect, compensate the plaintiff Xie Yeyang for medical expenses of RMB 1,623.24, transportation expenses of RMB 152, hospitalization food subsidy of RMB 11, nursing expenses of RMB 1,600, nutrition expenses of RMB 480, prosthetic costs incurred on December 13, 2011, of RMB 920, and disability compensation of RMB 25,470.40.

2. The defendant Shanghai Zoo shall, within ten days after this judgment takes effect, compensate the plaintiff Xie Yeyang for moral damages of RMB 2,000 and attorney's fees of RMB 2,000.

If the obligation to pay money is not fulfilled within the period specified in this judgment, interest on the debt for the period of delayed performance shall be doubled in accordance with Article 229 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China.

The judicial appraisal fees in this case amount to RMB 1,930, of which the plaintiff Xie Yeyang shall bear RMB 1,158 and the defendant Shanghai Zoo shall bear RMB 772.

The case acceptance fee is RMB 3,656.84. Due to the application of the summary procedure, the fee is halved to RMB 1,828.42, of which the plaintiff Xie Yeyang shall bear RMB 1,428.42 and the defendant Shanghai Zoo shall bear RMB 400.

Both Xie Yeyang and Shanghai Zoo disagreed with the first-instance judgment and appealed to the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court. Xie Yeyang's main grounds of appeal were: 1. Xie Yeyang was a 4-year-old child and could not clearly see or understand the content of the warning signs. Moreover, Shanghai Zoo did not provide evidence to prove that the warning signs were hung at the time of the incident. The duty rosters and other documents provided by the zoo were merely its internal rules and regulations, which were unilateral evidence provided by Shanghai Zoo and could not prove that it had fulfilled its patrol duties. 2. In this case, Shanghai Zoo failed to fulfill its obligation to inform and warn, failed to fulfill its patrol duties, and had safety hazards in its facilities and equipment. It should bear full tort liability. Since Xie Yeyang's legal representatives could not enter the metal protective railing to promptly carry Xie Yeyang out, they could not have foreseen the occurrence of such an incident and could not have promptly prevented the injury from happening. Therefore, they should not bear any responsibility in this case. 3. The prosthetic costs of Xie Yeyang were confirmed by a qualified rehabilitation assistive device production and assembly enterprise as inevitable expenses and should have been compensated in full at first instance. Therefore, Xie Yeyang requested the reversal of the original judgment and a judgment in support of all claims made at first instance.

The appellant Shanghai Zoo argued: It disagreed with the appellant Xie Yeyang's appeal claims. The majority of the facts found in the first-instance judgment were correct, except for the erroneous finding that the zoo was at fault. The prosthetic claimed by Xie Yeyang was cosmetic rather than functional and should not be supported.

Appellant Shanghai Zoo's main grounds of appeal: Shanghai Zoo had fulfilled its management obligations, including keeping the monkeys in cages in the primate house, installing safety isolation barriers for visitors, and posting multiple safety warning signs. The injury to Appellant Xie Yeyang occurred only because: first, he ignored the safety warning signs; second, he crossed the safety isolation barrier for visitors; third, he actively approached the iron cage or extended his limbs into the cage. If Xie Yeyang's legal representative had fulfilled their duty of care by instructing Xie Yeyang to visit civilly, preventing him from crossing the safety barrier, or preventing him from feeding the monkeys, and if just one of these measures had been taken, the injury to Xie Yeyang would not have occurred. Therefore, the corresponding liability should be borne by Xie Yeyang's legal representative. In addition, Xie Yeyang's prosthetic limb is a cosmetic prosthetic limb without functional features, and the cost thereof should not be borne by Shanghai Zoo. Accordingly, the appeal requests that the original judgment be reversed and that Xie Yeyang's claims at first instance be dismissed.

Appellant Xie Yeyang argued in response: The appellant zoo should bear full compensation liability and objected to its appellate claims.

Upon second instance trial, the Shanghai No.1 Intermediate People's Court confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The issues in dispute in this second instance are: First, whether the legal representative of Appellant Xie Yeyang and Appellant Shanghai Zoo each need to bear their respective liabilities for Xie Yeyang's injury, and how the liability should be apportioned; Second, whether the cost of Xie Yeyang's prosthetic limb should be included in the scope of compensation, and whether the subsequent maintenance costs should be resolved in this case.

The Shanghai No.1 Intermediate People's Court held in the second instance as follows:

Regarding the first issue in dispute, the court held that if an animal causes harm to another person, the animal's keeper or manager shall bear tort liability; however, if it can be proved that the harm was caused by the injured party's intentional conduct or gross negligence, the liability may be disclaimed or reduced. According to the facts found in this case, the cage in the primate house where the incident occurred was a closed iron mesh cage, with an additional metal isolation barrier outside the cage, and warning signs such as "No Crossing the Railing" were also hung on the cage. The metal isolation barrier, like the iron cage, served to prevent primates from harming visitors. It should be known to any person with civil capacity that crossing the isolation barrier while visiting the park is prohibited. Appellant Xie Yeyang, a four-year-old boy, was at an age of being active and lacking awareness of danger. While instructing Xie Yeyang on safe and civilized park visiting, his guardian should have strictly supervised him to prevent accidents. However, Xie Yeyang's guardian allowed him to leave their supervision, resulting in his crossing the protective barrier and feeding the monkeys, which led to the injury. Therefore, Xie Yeyang's guardian was grossly negligent. The court did not accept Xie Yeyang's argument that he bore no liability in this case. As for Appellant Shanghai Zoo, as an institution specialized in raising and managing animals, it has a higher duty of care and management compared to ordinary animal keepers. In addition to its warning function, the metal isolation barrier should also bear a certain isolating function. However, the 15 cm gap between the barriers could not completely prevent a young child from crawling through. Moreover, at the time of the incident, no zoo staff were present. After the incident, the zoo lacked an effective emergency contact method for visitors in need to reach the zoo, causing Xie Yeyang's side to be unable to promptly handle the emergency after the finger bite and had to seek treatment at a hospital on their own. Based on the above reasons, the court of first instance correctly found that Shanghai Zoo failed to fulfill its management duties. The court also did not accept Shanghai Zoo's appellate argument that it had fulfilled its management duties and should not bear compensation liability. Considering the fault of both parties, the court of first instance determined that Xie Yeyang's legal representative should bear 60% of the liability and Shanghai Zoo should bear 40% of the liability for Xie Yeyang's injury. This apportionment was reasonable, and the court affirmed it.

Regarding the second issue in dispute, the court held that Appellant Xie Yeyang is still young, and the partial loss of his right middle finger will indeed have some impact on his normal life and studies in the future. Although the prosthetic limb fitted is a cosmetic one, it can indeed serve a certain functional purpose. Therefore, the court of first instance, based on the degree of fault of both parties, properly exercised its discretion in supporting part of the prosthetic limb costs. The court did not accept Appellant Shanghai Zoo's argument that it should not bear the prosthetic limb costs. As the court of first instance noted, the future prosthetic limb costs have not yet actually occurred and are uncertain. To better protect Xie Yeyang's rights and interests, it was not improper to not support the future prosthetic limb costs at this time. The court also did not accept Xie Yeyang's argument that the future prosthetic limb costs should be resolved in this case. Xie Yeyang may separately assert such claims after the costs actually arise.

In summary, the judgment of the court of first instance was not improper and is affirmed. The appellate claims of both Appellant Xie Yeyang and Appellant Shanghai Zoo lack legal basis and are not supported by the court. Accordingly, pursuant to Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court rendered the following judgment on June 12, 2012:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed.

The appellate case acceptance fee is RMB 3,656.80, of which Appellant Xie Yeyang shall bear RMB 1,828.40 and Appellant Shanghai Zoo shall bear RMB 1,828.40.

This judgment is final.
